relevant_trials.title: Cabozantinib in Advanced Pancreatic Neuroendocrine and Carcinoid Tumors
relevant_trials.brief_summary:
Cabozantinib works by blocking the growth of new blood vessels that feed a tumor. In addition to blocking the formation of new blood cells in tumors, cabozantinib also blocks pathways that may be responsible for allowing cancers cells to become resistant to other "anti-angiogenic" drugs. Cabozantinib has been studied or is being study in research studies as a possible treatment for various types of cancer, including prostate cancer, brain cancer, thyroid cancer, lung cancer, and kidney cancer.

In this research study, the investigators wish to learn if cabozantinib is effective in treating patients with pancreatic neuroendocrine and carcinoid tumors.
relevant_trials.detailed_description:
Subjects will take cabozantinib orally, once per day, in cycles of 28 days.

During each cycle subjects will have the following procedures:

* Physical examination, including measurement of weight and vital signs
* Questions regarding any side effects
* Blood sample (about 1 tablespoon) for routine laboratory tests of blood cell counts, blood chemistries, organ function and blood clotting
* Blood sample (about 4 tablespoons) for research test to measure biomarkers to assess the response to study drug
* Urine sample for routine urine tests to monitor health

On Day 15 (beginning of week 3) during the first 3 cycles:

* Physical examination, including measurement of weight and vital signs
* Questions regarding any side effects
* Blood sample (about 1 tablespoon) for routine laboratory tests of blood cell counts, blood chemistries, organ function and blood clotting
* Blood sample (about 4 tablespoons) for research test to measure biomarkers to assess the response to study drug Subjects will receive a CT scan or MRI every two cycles (every two months) to evaluate disease.
relevant_trials.eligibility_criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* Locally unresectable or metastatic, histologically-confirmed, carcinoid or pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor. Tumors must be considered well- or moderately-differentiated. Patients with poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma or cell carcinoma are excluded from the study.
* A tumor sample is required for enrollment (except for patients diagnosed \> 7 years ago).
* Must have measurable disease by RECIST criteria
* Must have evidence of progressive disease within 12 months of study entry
* Prior or concurrent therapy with somatostatin analogs is permitted. If on somatostatin/octreotide, must be on a stable dose for at least two months.
* Age ≥ 18 years
* No major surgery or radiation in the prior 4 weeks prior to enrollment
* No prior therapy with cabozantinib
* ECOG Performance status ≤ 1
* Participants must have adequate organ and marrow function as defined below:

  * Absolute neutrophil count \> 1,500/mcL
  * Platelets \> 100,000/mcL
  * Total bilirubin \</= 1.5X normal institutional limits
  * AST (SGOT) and ALT (SGPT) \</=2.5x normal institutional limits, or \< 5x if liver metastases are present
  * Creatinine \</= 1.5x normal institutional limits or creatinine clearance \> 50mL/min
  * Urine Protein:Creatinine ratio of \<1
  * Lipase \< 1.5X upper limit of normal
  * Serum Albumin ≥ 2.8 g/dl
* Sexually active subjects must agree to use medically accepted methods of birth control during the course of the study and for 3 months following discontinuation of study treatments (excluding women who are not of child bearing potential and men who have been sterilized).
* Ability to understand and the willingness to sign a written informed consent document.

Exclusion Criteria

* Subjects receiving any other standard or investigational anticancer agents, with the exception of somatostatin/octreotide therapy. If patients has received prior cytotoxic chemotherapy, must be at least three weeks since last treatment before first dose of study treatment.
* Major surgery or radiation treatment \<4 weeks prior to enrollment. In addition, cannot have received radiation to the thorax or gastrointestinal tract within three months of the first dose of study treatment.
* Cannot have received radionuclide treatment within 6 weeks of first dose of study treatment.
* High grade or poorly differentiated neuroendocrine tumors
* Ongoing immunosuppression with systemic steroids or other immune modulator
* Presence of CNS metastatic disease

evaluation.explanation: This Phase II study is clinically relevant as it evaluates cabozantinib in patients with advanced, progressive pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (pNETs), aligning perfectly with the patient's diagnosis (G2 PanNET, Ki-67 15%) and current status (progression on prior therapies). The patient has progressed on sunitinib (VEGFR-TKI) and belzutifan; cabozantinib, a multi-kinase inhibitor targeting MET and VEGFR, represents a biologically rational subsequent line of systemic therapy, particularly if liver transplantation is deemed unfeasible due to the Ki-67 index (>10%) or if PRRT is not an option (e.g., low SSTR uptake). Although the automated search noted no results, the provided citations explicitly list the published "Phase II trial of cabozantinib in patients with carcinoid and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors," which provides the necessary efficacy and safety evidence to support considering this agent in the tumor board discussion for a heavily pre-treated patient.

relevant_trials.brief_summary: This study has 3 steps and not everyone will have all 3 steps done. The overall goals are to see if a new experimental drug is safe to image (step 1) and treat neuroendocrine tumors (step 2 and 3).
relevant_trials.eligibility_criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* Ability to understand and the willingness to sign a written informed consent document
* Adults ≥ 18 years old
* Histologically or cytologically confirmed metastatic and/or unresectable progressive, well differentiated carcinoid or pancreatic NET carcinoids
* Progressive metastatic disease defined by one of the following, occurring within 6 months of study entry:

  * At least a 20% increase in radiologically or clinically measurable disease
  * Appearance of any new lesion
  * Symptomatic disease (including worsening hormonal symptoms or symptoms related to tumor burden)
* Measurable disease as defined by RECIST 1.1.
* At least one metastasis must show uptake of 111In-DTPA-octreotide on SPECT that is higher than the physiologic radiotracer uptake by the liver
* ECOG performance status ≤ 2 (Karnofsky ≥ 60%)
* Patients must have normal organ and marrow function as defined below:

  * Leukocytes ≥ 3.0 x 109/L
  * Absolute neutrophil count (ANC) ≥ 1.5 x 10\^9/L
  * Hemoglobin ≥ 9.0 g/dL
  * Platelets ≥ 200 x 10\^9/L
  * Total bilirubin ≤ 1.25 x Upper Limit Normal (ULN)
  * AST (SGOT)/ ALT(SGPT) ≤ 2.5 x ULN with liver metastases
  * Alkaline phosphatase \< 2 x ULN (if known liver or bone disease)
  * Serum albumin \> 30 g/L, or serum albumin = 30 g/L but normal prothrombin time
  * Creatinine ≤ 1.5 x ULN or creatinine clearance (CrCl) calculated CrCl ≥ 60 mL/min/1.73m\^2
* Women of childbearing potential and men must agree to use adequate contraception prior to study entry and for the duration of study participation
* Previous local therapy (e.g., chemoembolization or bland embolization) is allowed if completed \> 6 weeks prior to study entry. For such patients, there must be either progression of measurable disease documented within the treatment field, or measurable progressive disease outside the treatment field prior to study entry.
* Previous chemotherapy and/or investigational agents are allowed if completed \> 4 weeks prior to study entry (\> 6 weeks if last regimen contained bis-chloroethyl nitrosourea (BCNU) or mitomycin C). For patients who received systemic therapy prior to study entry, there must be documented progression of measurable disease since receiving systemic therapy prior to study entry.
* Patients must not have disease that is currently amenable to surgery. Prior surgery is allowed no less than 6 weeks prior to study entry.

Exclusion Criteria:

* History of allergic reactions attributed to compounds of similar chemical or biologic composition to 177Lu-DOTA-JR11 as assessed from medical records
* Life expectancy \< 6 months as assessed by the treating physician.
* Treatment with short-acting somatostatin analogs less than 3 days and Sandostatin® depot injection less than 5 weeks before scanning and treatment
* Uncontrolled, intercurrent illness including, but not limited to, ongoing or active infection, symptomatic congestive heart failure, unstable angina pectoris, cardiac arrhythmia, or psychiatric illness/social situations that would limit compliance with study requirements
* Women who are pregnant or breastfeeding
* Toxicities from prior therapies that have not resolved to grade 1 or grade 0
* Known CNS metastases and/or carcinomatous meningitis
* Active malignancy of metastatic potential other than the known carcinoid or pancreatic NET within the past three years
* \>20% bone marrow external beam radiotherapy and/or previous radioisotope therapy

evaluation.explanation: This study provides meaningful clinical evidence supporting Peptide Receptor Radionuclide Therapy (PRRT) as a therapeutic alternative for this patient. The patient has a progressive, well-differentiated G2 Pancreatic NET and is currently failing belzutifan; while liver transplantation is being queried, she likely does not meet strict criteria (Ki-67 15% > 10% limit, active progression), making systemic options like PRRT the standard next line of care. The study evaluates 177Lu-satoreotide tetraxetan (an SSTR antagonist), with published results indicating positive safety and efficacy in metastatic Pan-NETs. This evidence reinforces the viability of PRRT as a robust non-surgical treatment path. Furthermore, the study's theranostic approach using 68Ga-DOTA-JR11 PET is clinically relevant for this patient, who requires high-sensitivity imaging to investigate new bone pain and rule out extrahepatic disease, a critical step in her management. I am assuming the patient's tumor is SSTR-positive, consistent with her G2 differentiation and prior response to somatostatin analogs.

relevant_trials.title: Study to Evaluate the Efficacy and Safety of Lutathera in Patients With Grade 2 and Grade 3 Advanced GEP-NET
relevant_trials.intervention: Lutathera; 30 mg Octreotide long acting repeatable (LAR) (Sandostatin LAR Depot); 2.5% Lys-Arg sterile amino acid solution; High dose 60 mg octreotide long-acting repeatable
relevant_trials.brief_summary: The aim of NETTER-2 was to determine if Lutathera in combination with long-acting octreotide prolongs progression free survival (PFS) in gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumor (GEP-NET) patients with high proliferation rate tumors (G2 and G3), when given as a first line treatment compared to treatment with high dose (60 mg) long-acting octreotide. Somatostatin analog (SSA) naive patients were eligible, as well as patients previously treated with SSAs in the absence of progression.
relevant_trials.detailed_description: The study consisted of a screening phase, a treatment phase, an optional cross-over phase for subjects assigned to the control arm, optional re-treatment phase for subjects assigned to the Lutathera arm, and a follow-up phase. This study compared treatment with Lutathera (7.4 GBq/200 mCi 4 × administrations every 8 weeks ± 1 week; cumulative dose: 29.6 GBq/800mCi) plus octreotide long-acting release (LAR) (30 mg every 8 weeks during Lutathera treatment and every 4 weeks after last Lutathera treatment) and high dose octreotide LAR (60 mg every 4 weeks).
relevant_trials.eligibility_criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* Presence of metastasized or locally advanced, inoperable (curative intent) histologically proven, well differentiated Grade 2 or Grade 3 gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine (GEP-NET) tumor diagnosed within 6 months prior to screening.
* Ki67 index ≥10 and ≤ 55%
* Patients ≥ 15 years of age and a body weight of \> 40 kg at screening
* Expression of somatostatin receptors on all target lesions documented by CT/MRI scans, assessed by any of the following somatostatin receptor imaging (SRI) modalities within 3 months prior to randomization: \[68Ga\]-DOTA-TOC (e.g. Somakit-TOC®) PET/CT (or MRI when applicable based on target lesions) imaging, \[68Ga\]-DOTA-TATE PET/CT (or MRI when applicable based on target lesions) imaging (e.g. NETSPOT®), Somatostatin Receptor scintigraphy (SRS) with \[111In\]-pentetreotide (Octreoscan® SPECT/CT), SRS with \[99mTc\]-Tektrotyd, \[64Cu\]-DOTA-TATE PET/CT (or MRI when applicable based on target lesions) imaging.
* The tumor uptake observed in the target lesions must be \> normal liver uptake.
* Karnofsky Performance Score (KPS) ≥ 60
* Presence of at least 1 measurable site of disease
* Patients who have provided a signed informed consent form to participate in the study, obtained prior to the start of any protocol related activities

Exclusion Criteria:

* Creatinine clearance \< 40 mL/min calculated by the Cockroft Gault method
* Hb concentration \< 5.0 mmol/L (\<8.0 g/dL); WBC \< 2x10E9/L (2000/mm3); platelets \< 75x10E9/L (75x10E3/mm3)
* Total bilirubin \> 3 x ULN
* Serum albumin \< 3.0 g/dL unless prothrombin time is within the normal range
* Pregnancy or lactation
* Women of child-bearing potential, defined as all women physiologically capable of becoming pregnant, are not allowed to participate in this study UNLESS they are using highly effective methods of contraception throughout the study treatment period (including cross-over and re-treatment, if applicable) and for 7 months after study drug discontinuation
* Peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT) at any time prior to randomization in the study.
* Documented RECIST progression to previous treatments for the current GEP-NET at any time prior to randomization
* Patients for whom in the opinion of the investigator other therapeutic options (eg chemo-, targeted therapy) are considered more appropriate than therapy offered in the study, based on patient and disease characteristics
* Any previous therapy with Interferons, Everolimus (mTOR-inhibitors), chemotherapy or other systemic therapies for GEP-NET administered for more than 1 month or within 12 weeks prior to randomization in the study.
* Any previous radioembolization, chemoembolization and radiofrequency ablation for GEP-NET
* Any surgery within 12 weeks prior to randomization in the study
* Known brain metastases, unless these metastases have been treated and stabilized for at least 24 weeks, prior to screening in the study. Patients with a history of brain metastases must have a head CT or MRI with contrast to document stable disease prior to randomization in the study.
* Uncontrolled congestive heart failure (NYHA II, III, IV). Patients with history of congestive heart failure who do not violate this exclusion criterion will undergo an evaluation of their cardiac ejection fraction prior to randomization via echocardiography. The results from an earlier assessment (not exceeding 30 days prior to randomization) may substitute the evaluation at the discretion of the Investigator, if no clinical worsening is noted. The patient's measured cardiac ejection fraction in these patients must be ≥40% before randomization.
* QTcF \> 470 msec for females and QTcF \> 450 msec for males or congenital long QT syndrome
* Uncontrolled diabetes mellitus as defined by hemoglobin A1c value \> 7.5%
* Hyperkaleamia \> 6.0 mmol/L (CTCAE Grade 3) which is not corrected prior to study enrolment
* Any patient receiving treatment with short-acting octreotide, which cannot be interrupted for 24 h before and 24 h after the administration of Lutathera, or any patient receiving treatment with SSAs (e.g. octreotide long-acting), which cannot be interrupted for at least 6 weeks before the administration of Lutathera.
* Patients with any other significant medical, psychiatric, or surgical condition, currently uncontrolled by treatment, which may interfere with the completion of the study.
* Prior external beam radiation therapy to more than 25% of the bone marrow.
* Current spontaneous urinary incontinence
* Other known co-existing malignancies except non-melanoma skin cancer and carcinoma in situ of the uterine cervix, unless definitively treated and proven no evidence of recurrence for 5 years
* Patient with known incompatibility to CT Scans with IV contrast due to allergic reaction or renal insufficiency. If such a patient can be imaged with MRI, then the patient would not be excluded.
* Hypersensitivity to any somatostatin analogues, the IMPs active substance or to any of the excipients.
* Patients who have participated in any therapeutic clinical study/received any investigational agent within the last 30 days

publications.title: [177Lu]Lu-DOTA-TATE plus long-acting octreotide versus high‑dose long-acting octreotide for the treatment of newly diagnosed, advanced grade 2-3, well-differentiated, gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumours (NETTER-2): an open-label, randomised, phase 3 study.
publications.abstract_text: There are currently no standard first-line treatment options for patients with higher grade 2-3, well-differentiated, advanced, gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumours. We aimed to investigate the efficacy and safety of first-line [ 177 Lu]Lu-DOTA-TATE ( 177 Lu-Dotatate) treatment.
publications.full_content: Full text links Cite Display options Display options Format Abstract PubMed PMID Abstract Background: There are currently no standard first-line treatment options for patients with higher grade 2-3, well-differentiated, advanced, gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumours. We aimed to investigate the efficacy and safety of first-line [ 177 Lu]Lu-DOTA-TATE ( 177 Lu-Dotatate) treatment. Methods: NETTER-2 was an open-label, randomised, parallel-group, superiority, phase 3 trial. We enrolled patients (aged ≥15 years) with newly diagnosed higher grade 2 (Ki67 ≥10% and ≤20%) and grade 3 (Ki67 >20% and ≤55%), somatostatin receptor-positive (in all target lesions), advanced gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumours from 45 centres across nine countries in North America, Europe, and Asia. We used interactive response technologies to randomly assign (2:1) patients to receive four cycles (cycle interval was 8 weeks ± 1 week) of intravenous 177 Lu-Dotatate plus intramuscular octreotide 30 mg long-acting repeatable (LAR) then octreotide 30 mg LAR every 4 weeks ( 177 Lu-Dotatate group) or high-dose octreotide 60 mg LAR every 4 weeks (control group), stratified by neuroendocrine tumour grade (2 vs 3) and origin (pancreas vs other). Tumour assessments were done at baseline, week 16, and week 24, and then every 12 weeks until disease progression or death. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival by blinded, independent, central radiology assessment. We did the primary analysis at 101 progression-free survival events as the final progression-free survival analysis. NETTER-2 is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT03972488 , and is active and not recruiting. Findings: Between Jan 22, 2020, and Oct 13, 2022, we screened 261 patients, 35 (13%) of whom were excluded. We randomly assigned 226 (87%) patients (121 [54%] male and 105 [46%] female) to the 177 Lu-Dotatate group (n=151 [67%]) and control group (n=75 [33%]). Median progression-free survival was 8·5 months (95% CI 7·7-13·8) in the control group and 22·8 months (19·4-not estimated) in the 177 Lu-Dotatate group (stratified hazard ratio 0·276 [0·182-0·418]; p<0·0001). During the treatment period, adverse events (of any grade) occurred in 136 (93%) of 147 treated patients in the 177 Lu-Dotatate group and 69 (95%) of 73 treated patients in the control group. There were no study drug-related deaths during the treatment period. Interpretation: First-line 177 Lu-Dotatate plus octreotide LAR significantly extended median progression-free survival (by 14 months) in patients with grade 2 or 3 advanced gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumours. 177 Lu-Dotatate should be considered a new standard of care in first-line therapy in this population. publications.full_content: Full text links Cite Display options Display options Format Abstract PubMed PMID Abstract Purpose of review: Neuroendocrine neoplasms (NENs) are rare and heterogeneous malignancies whose natural evolution may be defined according to various prognostic factors, including localization of the primitive tumour, hormone secretory status, histological grade, tumour burden, tumour growth rate, expression of somatostatin receptors and fluorodeoxyglucose-avidity. The treatment of these tumours in an advanced setting is based on relatively little robust data. Recent findings: A recent pathological classification introduced a new category of high-grade but well differentiated neuroendocrine tumours (NET G3), with markedly different behaviour from neuroendocrine carcinomas (NECs). Yet, the optimal treatment of those tumours is still uncertain. Advances are needed in molecular subtyping of NENs to understand better their heterogeneity and inform personalized therapies. Summary: The current review summarizes the current knowledge, indicates some exciting future directions and outlines the most interesting ongoing clinical trials likely to impact current practice. publications.full_content: Full text links Cite Display options Display options Format Abstract PubMed PMID Abstract The incidence of neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) in the US is rising, with 8.3 cases per 100,000 individuals diagnosed in 2018 compared with 6.98 cases per 100,000 individuals diagnosed in 2012. 1,2 Most patients with NETs are diagnosed with metastatic disease, at which point curative surgery is no longer a treatment option. 3 Prior to 2017, available treatments for advanced NETs included somatostatin analogues (lanreotide [Somatuline] and octreotide [Sandostatin]), targeted therapy (everolimus [Afinitor] and sunitinib [Sutent]), and chemotherapy. 4-7 In 2017, the World Health Organization added a classification for well-differentiated grade 3 NETs (Ki67 > 20% and ≤ 55%). 8 Previously these tumors were placed under the umbrella of poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinomas. Given that well-differentiated grade 3 NETs are relatively new, standard-of-care treatment options are undefined. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03972488 . evaluation.explanation: The NETTER-2 study provides highly relevant evidence for this patient with a Grade 2 (Ki-67 15%) pancreatic NET. Biologically, the patient fits perfectly into the study's specific cohort of 'higher Grade 2' (Ki-67 10-20%) and Grade 3 well-differentiated GEP-NETs, a population where PRRT efficacy was previously less defined. Although the patient is heavily pre-treated (sunitinib, lanreotide, belzutifan) and the study focused on the first-line setting, the robust outcomes (median PFS 22.8 months, HR 0.276) confirm that tumors with this specific proliferation index are highly sensitive to 177Lu-Dotatate. Assuming the patient demonstrates SSTR uptake on the recommended PET scan, this evidence directly supports the clinical assessment's consideration of PRRT as a viable alternative to liver transplantation (which is likely unfeasible due to Ki-67 >10%) or systemic chemotherapy. The study validates the biological rationale for using PRRT in this specific Ki-67 range.
evaluation.trial_title: Study to Evaluate the Efficacy and Safety of Lutathera in Patients With Grade 2 and Grade 3 Advanced GEP-NET

all_evaluations.explanation: The study aligns biologically as it specifically investigated patients with G2-3 well-differentiated GEP-NETs, directly matching the patient's diagnosis of a G2 (Ki-67 15%) pancreatic NET. In the clinical context of a patient progressing after multiple lines of therapy (SSA, sunitinib, TAE, belzutifan) where later-line options are being considered, this study provides crucial evidence regarding the utility of immunotherapy. The published results (Chan et al., 2022) reported an objective response rate (ORR) of 0% and a median progression-free survival of only 3.3 months, concluding that single-agent avelumab has limited antitumor activity in this population. This negative evidence is highly clinically relevant as it informs the treatment decision to avoid ineffective single-agent PD-L1 blockade, thereby guiding the recommendation toward more proven alternatives such as PRRT (assuming SSTR-PET positivity) or systemic chemotherapy (e.g., streptozotocin/temozolomide) for this patient.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Avelumab in G2-3 NET

all_evaluations.explanation: This study does not provide meaningful clinical evidence to guide therapy recommendations for this patient. It is a broad observational registry focused on establishing infrastructure for real-world data (RWD) and biomarker testing across all advanced malignancies, rather than a prospective trial testing a specific intervention for Neuroendocrine Neoplasms (NENs). The provided publications are methodological papers discussing the concepts of Master Protocols, Real-World Evidence, and genomic databases (e.g., AACR Project GENIE) rather than reporting clinical outcomes for specific NET treatments. As there are no specific efficacy or safety results regarding pancreatic NET therapies (such as PRRT, chemotherapy, or liver transplantation) derived from this registry, it fails the criterion for Evidence Quality and Relevance.
all_evaluations.trial_title: The Registry of Oncology Outcomes Associated with Testing and Treatment

all_evaluations.explanation: The study does not provide meaningful evidence for this patient's current treatment decisions because she has already received and progressed on the studied intervention (Lanreotide). The patient was treated with Lanreotide and Sunitinib starting in 2018 and has since experienced disease progression requiring multiple subsequent lines of therapy (TAE, Belzutifan). This prospective observational study evaluates the real-world efficacy of Lanreotide in patients who are generally SSA-naive or stable on therapy, explicitly excluding those who progressed between initiation and enrollment. As the patient has already failed this therapy, general efficacy data for Lanreotide in earlier lines does not inform her current management options, which revolve around liver transplantation, PRRT, or systemic chemotherapy.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Community-based Neuroendocrine Tumor (NET) Research Study

all_evaluations.explanation: This study does not provide meaningful evidence for therapy recommendations because it is an observational biomarker study focused on validating circulating tumor cells (CTCs) and ctDNA as monitoring tools, rather than a therapeutic trial evaluating treatment efficacy. While the disease biology (Pancreatic NET) aligns with the patient's diagnosis, the study aims to correlate biomarkers with disease course during standard treatments (like everolimus) rather than testing a specific intervention's outcomes. Consequently, it does not offer actionable clinical data to guide the complex therapeutic decisions facing this patient, such as the feasibility of liver transplantation versus initiating PRRT or systemic chemotherapy.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Circulating Tumor Cells and Tumor DNA in HCC and NET

all_evaluations.explanation: The study fails the Treatment Context and Clinical Applicability criterion. The patient previously underwent a distal pancreatectomy in 2018, removing the primary tumor. This study evaluates a specific surgical technique (minimally invasive enucleation with pancreatic duct repair) for localized, solitary pancreatic tumors eligible for parenchyma-sparing resection. Since the patient's primary tumor has already been resected and she currently presents with metastatic liver progression requiring systemic therapy or liver-directed options (such as liver transplantation or PRRT), evidence regarding surgical enucleation of the primary site is anatomically impossible to apply and clinically irrelevant to her current management.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Minimally Invasive Pancreatic Enucleation With Main Pancreatic Duct Exposure, Repair or Reconstruction

all_evaluations.explanation: The study provides meaningful evidence for this patient because it evaluates the real-world effectiveness and safety of Lutathera (177Lu-DOTATATE) in patients with progressive, well-differentiated (G1-G2) GEP-NETs, directly aligning with the patient's diagnosis of a progressive G2 Pan-NET (Ki-67 15%). Clinically, the patient is progressing on belzutifan and is likely ineligible for liver transplantation due to her Ki-67 index (>10%) and active progression; thus, she requires a new line of systemic therapy. Assuming the patient demonstrates SSTR uptake on the recommended PET scan, PRRT is a standard-of-care consideration. The study is particularly relevant as it includes a high proportion of G2 patients (71%), offering specific insights into outcomes for this subgroup that may differ from the G1-predominant populations in earlier pivotal trials. This prospective real-world evidence supports the clinical decision to transition the patient to PRRT.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Italian Prospective Observational Study Assessing the Effectiveness and Outcomes Associated With Lutathera Treatment in GEP-NETs

all_evaluations.explanation: The study fails the Treatment Context and Evidence Relevance criteria. While the disease biology (low-grade pancreatic tumor) aligns, the study evaluates postoperative pancreatic fistula risks specifically following minimally invasive enucleation (MIEN) of primary tumors. This patient underwent a total gastrectomy and distal pancreatectomy in 2018, meaning her primary tumor has already been resected via a standard oncological resection, not enucleation. Furthermore, her current clinical need involves managing metastatic liver progression (evaluating liver transplantation vs. systemic therapies like PRRT or chemotherapy). Evidence regarding surgical complications of a primary tumor procedure she is not a candidate for (and has already bypassed) offers no actionable insights for her current metastatic disease management.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Pancreatic Fistula After Minimally Invasive Enucleation

all_evaluations.explanation: The study does not meet the criteria for clinical applicability or disease alignment. The patient has known metastatic disease (M1) with bilobar liver metastases and has already undergone resection of the primary tumor in 2018. In contrast, this study recruits patients with clinically non-metastatic (cM0) disease undergoing primary tumor resection to evaluate the utility of intraoperative ultrasound in detecting occult liver metastases. The study's focus on staging patients thought to be localized is not relevant to a patient with established, progressing metastatic disease currently being evaluated for liver transplantation or systemic therapy (PRRT/chemotherapy). Furthermore, the provided publications appear to be background literature rather than results from this specific prospective cohort (2020-2023), offering no actionable evidence to guide decision-making for this specific case.
all_evaluations.trial_title: The Role of Intraoperative Hepatic Ultrasonography in Gastrointestinal or Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumor

all_evaluations.explanation: The study meets the criteria for **Disease/Biology Alignment** (G2 PanNET) and **Treatment Context** (PRRT is a relevant consideration for SSTR-positive disease progressing on targeted therapies like belzutifan, assuming SSTR-positivity as per clinical assumptions). However, it fails the **Evidence Quality and Relevance** criterion. The only published results provided focus exclusively on radiation dosimetry, external dose rates, and discharge timing guidelines for radiation protection. There is no reported data on therapeutic efficacy (e.g., Progression-Free Survival, Objective Response Rate) or clinical safety profiles (e.g., hematotoxicity, nephrotoxicity) in the provided input. Without efficacy or clinical outcome data, this study cannot inform the therapeutic decision-making process (i.e., weighing PRRT against alternatives like chemotherapy or liver transplantation) for this patient.
all_evaluations.trial_title: A Study Comparing Treatment With Lutetium[177Lu] Oxodotreotide Injection to Octreotide LAR in Patients With GEP-NETs

all_evaluations.explanation: The study does not provide meaningful evidence for therapy recommendations for this patient. While the disease biology (GEP-NET G1/G2) aligns, the study fails on treatment context and evidence relevance. OPERA is a non-interventional study evaluating patient perception of information and quality of life specifically upon *initiating* lanreotide. This patient initiated and subsequently progressed on lanreotide years ago (2018) and is currently in a late-line setting (post-sunitinib, post-TAE, post-belzutifan) evaluating complex options like liver transplantation, PRRT, or chemotherapy. Evidence regarding information perception during the initiation of a standard first-line therapy that the patient has already exhausted offers no actionable insights for selecting among the current therapeutic alternatives (transplant vs. PRRT vs. chemo).
all_evaluations.trial_title: Perception of Information and Quality of Life in Neuroendocrine Tumour on Lanreotide Autogel

all_evaluations.explanation: The study does not meet the criteria for Evidence Quality and Relevance regarding this specific patient. While the AcSé Pembrolizumab trial design includes a cohort for rare neuroendocrine tumors (NETs), the provided published results (PMID: 37429302) exclusively report findings for the 'rare and ultra-rare sarcomas' subgroup (e.g., chordoma, alveolar soft part sarcoma). There are no efficacy or safety data provided for the NET cohort in the input. Evidence of pembrolizumab activity in sarcomas cannot be biologically or clinically extrapolated to guide therapy for a well-differentiated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor (Pan-NET), which is a distinct biological entity. Without results specific to the NET cohort, this study offers no actionable evidence to inform the patient's treatment plan.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Secured Access to Pembrolizumab for Patients With Selected Rare Cancer Types

all_evaluations.explanation: This Phase 3 COMPETE trial provides critical evidence for guiding the next line of therapy for this patient. Biologically, the patient aligns perfectly with the study population: progressive, well-differentiated G2 Pan-NET (Ki-67 15%). Clinically, the patient is progressing on belzutifan and is likely ineligible for liver transplantation due to Ki-67 >10% and active progression. She requires a new systemic therapy and is naive to both interventions tested in this study (PRRT and everolimus), having previously received only sunitinib and lanreotide. Assuming SSTR-positivity (standard for G2 NETs and required for eligibility), this study offers direct, high-quality evidence that 177Lu-edotreotide significantly improves PFS compared to everolimus (23.9 vs 14.1 months, HR 0.67). This result is immediately actionable, suggesting PRRT may be the superior choice over everolimus for her next line of treatment, especially given the need to control extrahepatic disease if bone metastases are confirmed.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Efficacy and Safety of 177Lu-edotreotide PRRT in GEP-NET Patients

all_evaluations.explanation: The study does not provide meaningful evidence to guide the specific therapeutic recommendations for this patient. While the disease biology (well-differentiated GEP-NET) and context (surgical intervention) align, the study is designed to validate a biomarker (NETest) for monitoring disease status and recurrence post-surgery, rather than evaluating the efficacy or safety of a therapeutic intervention itself. The patient's primary clinical dilemma involves determining the feasibility of liver transplantation versus systemic alternatives (e.g., PRRT, chemotherapy) given her Ki-67 index (15%) and recent progression, which conflict with standard transplant criteria. Evidence regarding the utility of a blood-based transcript assay does not address these specific biological contraindications or inform the comparative effectiveness of transplantation versus other active therapies.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Surgical Intervention and the NETest

all_evaluations.explanation: The study does not meet the Disease/Biology Alignment criterion. The patient has a well-differentiated (G2) pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor (Pan-NET), whereas this Phase 2 trial (NCT03333616) specifically evaluates nivolumab plus ipilimumab in rare genitourinary (GU) malignancies, including high-grade neuroendocrine carcinomas of the GU tract. There is a fundamental biological mismatch between well-differentiated gastroenteropancreatic NETs and high-grade GU neuroendocrine carcinomas or other rare GU tumors (e.g., adrenocortical carcinoma, bladder variants). Evidence regarding the efficacy of checkpoint inhibitors in high-grade GU tumors cannot be reasonably extrapolated to inform treatment for a well-differentiated pancreatic NET due to distinct tumor microenvironments and mutational burdens. Consequently, the study results do not provide actionable clinical insights for this patient's care.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Nivolumab Combined With Ipilimumab for Patients With Advanced Rare Genitourinary Tumors

all_evaluations.explanation: The study is not currently relevant for informing therapy recommendations for this patient. While the study demonstrates the efficacy of entrectinib in *NTRK/ROS1/ALK* fusion-positive solid tumors and includes specific evidence of activity in neuroendocrine neoplasms (Sigal et al.), these genomic alterations are extremely rare in pancreatic NETs (<1%). Unlike SSTR expression, which is highly probable (>90%) and assumed positive for well-differentiated NETs, it is not clinically reasonable to assume this patient harbors an *NTRK* fusion without specific molecular profiling results. Consequently, the study population (fusion-driven malignancy) is not biologically concordant with the patient's current known status (unselected Pan-NET). Given the patient's progression on belzutifan and ineligibility for liver transplantation (due to Ki-67 >10% and active progression), the evidence does not support recommending entrectinib over standard, high-probability alternatives such as PRRT or chemotherapy (e.g., CAPTEM). The study would only become relevant if subsequent genomic testing confirmed a fusion.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Basket Study of Entrectinib (RXDX-101) for the Treatment of Patients With Solid Tumors Harboring NTRK 1/2/3 (Trk A/B/C), ROS1, or ALK Gene Rearrangements (Fusions)

all_evaluations.explanation: The study aligns with the patient's disease biology (metastatic pancreatic NET with liver-dominant disease) and clinical context, as liver-directed therapies are a standard consideration for progressive liver metastases and the patient has previously responded to TAE. However, the provided study data consists solely of a study protocol (Chen et al., 2018) outlining the design of the RETNET trial without reporting any completed efficacy or safety results. Without published outcomes comparing the embolization techniques (Bland vs. TACE vs. DEB-TACE), the study does not provide actionable evidence (Criterion 3) to inform whether re-embolization or a specific technique would be beneficial for this patient after her progression on belzutifan.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Randomized Embolization Trial for NeuroEndocrine Tumor Metastases to the Liver

all_evaluations.explanation: The study is not relevant because it specifically evaluates the efficacy of Temozolomide-Capecitabine (TEMCAP) in **Grade 3** (Ki-67 >20%) gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, whereas the patient has a **Grade 2** (Ki-67 15%) pancreatic NET. Although CAPTEM is a clinically appropriate consideration for the patient's progressive disease (as noted in the assessment), the evidence supporting its use in G2 tumors is established by prior research (e.g., Strosberg et al., cited in the study background) rather than this specific trial. The trial's goal is to extend the indication to G3 tumors, a population with distinct biological behavior and prognosis compared to the patient's G2 disease. Therefore, the results of this study do not provide applicable evidence to inform the management of this specific patient.
all_evaluations.trial_title: TEMCAP in Grade 3 and Low Ki-67 Gastroenteropancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumors

all_evaluations.explanation: This study is a retrospective database (registry) rather than an interventional trial evaluating a specific therapy. The provided publications (dated 2008–2018) predate the study registration (2021) and represent general background literature—such as epidemiology (Yao 2008, Dasari 2017) and pathology classification of G3 neoplasms (Tang 2016, Raj 2017)—rather than outcomes derived from this specific registry. As the patient has a G2 PanNET and requires decision-making support for next-line therapy (e.g., liver transplantation vs. PRRT vs. chemotherapy) after progressing on belzutifan, this entry offers no actionable prospective evidence or specific treatment outcome data to guide clinical management.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Multicenter Retrospective Database on Prognostic and Predictive Factors in Patients With Neuroendocrine Tumors

all_evaluations.explanation: The study does not provide meaningful clinical evidence to guide treatment for this patient because it lacks published results. While the ANTARES trial (NCT06638931) includes neuroendocrine tumors and addresses a relevant clinical context (progression on standard therapies), the provided data explicitly states 'No detailed findings available' for this specific trial. The listed publications are background references to unrelated major trials (e.g., KEYNOTE-158, DESTINY-Breast03) or methodology papers, not outcomes from the ANTARES cohort. Without specific efficacy or safety data from this study, it cannot inform therapeutic decisions or validate the use of nivolumab for this patient's well-differentiated pancreatic NET, particularly given that single-agent immunotherapy is not standard for G2 NETs without specific biomarkers (e.g., MSI-H) which are not confirmed here.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Agnostic Therapy in Rare Solid Tumors

all_evaluations.explanation: This Phase 2 study of 212Pb-DOTAMTATE (AlphaMedix) is highly relevant for this patient with a metastatic G2 pancreatic NET who is progressing on belzutifan. Biologically, the patient's disease aligns with the study population of SSTR-positive GEP-NETs (assuming typical SSTR positivity for G2 NETs). Clinically, the patient is PRRT-naive, matching Cohort 1 of the study. The published results demonstrate a remarkably high Objective Response Rate (ORR) of 56.8% in PRRT-naive patients, which is superior to historical controls for standard 177Lu-DOTATATE. Given the patient's liver-dominant disease and the previous consideration of liver transplantation (which requires disease control/stability), a therapy with a high probability of inducing objective tumor shrinkage is particularly valuable. This evidence supports considering targeted alpha therapy as a potent alternative to standard beta-PRRT or chemotherapy in the sequence of treatment.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Targeted Alpha-emitter Therapy of PRRT Naïve and Previous PRRT Neuroendocrine Tumor Patients

all_evaluations.explanation: This study provides meaningful evidence for the patient's potential next line of therapy. The patient has a progressive, well-differentiated G2 Pancreatic NET (Ki-67 15%), which aligns with the study's inclusion criteria (well-differentiated NETs, Ki-67 <20%). While the patient is currently being evaluated for liver transplantation, she is progressing on belzutifan, making Peptide Receptor Radionuclide Therapy (PRRT) with Lu-177 DOTATATE a clinically relevant alternative or subsequent option, as noted in the assessment. Assuming SSTR-PET positivity (typical for G2 NETs), the study is highly applicable. The published results are particularly relevant because they identify specific survival predictors—such as the presence of ≥5 bone metastases and high liver tumor burden (>50%)—that correlate with poor outcomes. Given the patient's reported bone pain and need for liver burden assessment, these findings offer actionable prognostic information to guide the decision between PRRT, chemotherapy, or continued pursuit of surgical options.
all_evaluations.trial_title: An Open Label Registry Study of Lutetium-177 (DOTA0, TYR3) Octreotate (Lu-DOTA-TATE) Treatment in Patients with Somatostatin Receptor Positive Tumours

all_evaluations.explanation: The study does not meet the criteria for clinical applicability or disease alignment. The patient underwent a distal pancreatectomy in 2018, removing the primary tumor; therefore, there is no pancreatic lesion to target with the study intervention (EUS-guided radiofrequency ablation of pancreatic neoplasms). Furthermore, the study is designed for patients with localized, small (<25mm), low-grade (Ki-67 ≤5%) tumors without distant metastases. This contrasts sharply with the patient's status, which involves metastatic disease (bilobar liver metastases, possible bone involvement) and a higher Ki-67 index (15%). Evidence regarding local ablation of primary pancreatic tumors cannot inform the management of a patient with a resected primary and progressive metastatic disease.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Endoscopic Ultrasound-guided RadioFrequency Ablation for the Treatment Pancreatic NeuroEndocrine Neoplasms

all_evaluations.explanation: The study (NCT02923934) included a cohort of neuroendocrine tumors, but the specific published results provided in the input (Klein et al., JAMA Oncol 2020) report exclusively on the Biliary Tract Cancer (BTC) subgroup. Evidence derived from biliary tract cancers (cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder carcinoma) is not biologically transferable to this patient's well-differentiated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor (PanNET, G2). While the trial's NET cohort was published separately (cited as a similar article), the provided key findings describe outcomes (ORR 23%, DCR 44%) specific to BTC, which cannot inform therapy for a neuroendocrine malignancy. Furthermore, immunotherapy is not currently a standard treatment for G2 PanNETs, and without specific efficacy data for the NET cohort provided in the structured fields, this source does not offer actionable evidence to guide treatment decisions for this patient.
all_evaluations.trial_title: A Phase II Trial of Ipilimumab and Nivolumab for the Treatment of Rare Cancers

all_evaluations.explanation: The study does not meet the criteria for disease alignment or clinical applicability. The patient has a metastatic well-differentiated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor (Pan-NET G2) with liver metastases. The study (NCT03110978) investigates Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy (SABR) combined with Nivolumab specifically for early-stage (Stage I-IIA) or recurrent Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC). While the study inclusion criteria mention NSCLC with neuroendocrine features or atypical carcinoids, the primary disease site (lung vs. pancreas), stage (localized/early vs. metastatic), and biological context are fundamentally different. Evidence regarding the efficacy of SABR plus immunotherapy in early-stage lung cancer cannot be extrapolated to guide treatment for metastatic pancreatic NETs, where checkpoint inhibitors (like nivolumab) generally have limited efficacy in well-differentiated G2 tumors and the clinical focus is on liver-directed therapies or systemic agents like PRRT or chemotherapy.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy With or Without Nivolumab in Treating Patients With Stage I-IIA or Recurrent Non-small Cell Lung Cancer

all_evaluations.explanation: The study does not meet the criterion for Treatment Context/Clinical Applicability. This study evaluates Lanreotide Autogel in Asian patients with GEP-NETs, primarily in early treatment settings (inclusion requires <5 months of prior Lanreotide). The patient has already received Lanreotide (in combination with sunitinib) starting in 2018 and has since progressed through multiple lines of therapy, including liver-directed therapies and belzutifan. Evidence confirming the efficacy of first-line somatostatin analogs does not provide actionable insights for a patient who has already developed resistance to this drug class and is currently seeking salvage options (e.g., liver transplantation, PRRT, or chemotherapy) for progressive disease.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Asian Investigation of Lanreotide Autogel® in the Management of GEP-NETs

all_evaluations.explanation: This Phase II study provides meaningful evidence for a biomarker-driven treatment option in well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors. The patient aligns with the study population (metastatic G2 PanNET, progressive disease), and although her Estrogen/Progesterone Receptor (ER/PR) status is currently unknown, the study establishes that ~30% of NETs express these receptors. Given the patient is heavily pre-treated (SSA, Sunitinib, TAE, Belzutifan) and likely ineligible for liver transplantation due to progression and Ki-67 >10%, she requires salvage therapy options. The study demonstrates that Tamoxifen is safe and yields a disease control rate of 56.5% with a median PFS of 7.9 months in ER/PR-positive patients. This evidence supports a clinical recommendation to perform IHC staining for ER/PR on her tumor tissue; if positive, Tamoxifen offers a viable, low-toxicity alternative to systemic chemotherapy or PRRT.
all_evaluations.trial_title: Study of Tamoxifen in Well Differentiated Neuroendocrine Tumors and Hormone Receptor Positive Expression

all_evaluations.explanation: The study meets all criteria for clinical relevance. Biologically, the patient's Grade 2 pancreatic NET (Ki-67 15%) aligns perfectly with the study's pNET cohort (Grade 1-2).
